passages.text: ERYSIPELAS, or ST ANTHONY'S FIRE, an inflammation of the skin, with a red, hot and shining swelling, which spreads irregularly, and is attended with fever.
It attacks the face more often than any other part, and the swollen skin often rises in small blisters filled with a yellowish fluid.
When it attacks the head it is often attended with delirium, and sometimes proves fatal.
The cause is commonly thought to be an acrid bile, thrown upon the skin from a disordered state of the stomach and liver.
It has the name of St Anthony's fire from the saint who was invoked against it in the middle ages.
In hospitals it often follows wounds and operations, and passes from one patient to another, so that whole wards are sometimes affected.
The cure consists in bleeding, in purging with saline medicines, and a cooling diet; cold applications to the part are hurtful, as they may drive the disease inwards.
Erysipelas is a bacterial infection of the upper layers of the skin. It causes a raised, well-defined, bright red rash, typically on the face or legs, often with fever.
The affected skin is swollen, warm and tender, and it may form blisters.
Most cases are caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, also called group A streptococcus.
The bacteria usually enter through a break in the skin, such as a wound, a scratch or a surgical cut.
The usual treatment is an antibiotic, most often penicillin.
Complications are uncommon but can include abscess, spread of the infection into deeper tissue, and sepsis.
Erysipelas was historically called St Anthony's fire. The same name was also used for ergotism, a different illness caused by eating rye infected with a fungus.

reasons: Same headword in both: ERYSIPELAS and Erysipelas.
Rare terms appear in both: St Anthony's fire, shining red swelling, blisters, wounds.
Ergotism scores because it shares the name St Anthony's fire, but it is a different disease.

britannica.quote: a red, hot and shining swelling

wikipedia.quote: a raised, well-defined, bright red rash

alignments.label: The face

britannica.quote: It attacks the face more often than any other part

wikipedia.quote: typically on the face or legs

alignments.note: Wikipedia names the face and the legs. The 1810 entry names only the face.

alignments.label: Blisters
alignments.note: Same observation. The fact did not change.

alignments.label: Acrid bile

britannica.quote: an acrid bile, thrown upon the skin

wikipedia.quote: Most cases are caused by Streptococcus pyogenes

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. A bacterium causes the disease, not bile from the stomach and liver.

alignments.label: St Anthony's fire

britannica.quote: It has the name of St Anthony's fire

wikipedia.quote: The same name was also used for ergotism

alignments.note: A language point. The name was used for erysipelas, but also for ergotism, a different disease from poisoned rye. Inference: the medieval cult of St Anthony was linked mainly to ergotism, so the 1810 story of the name is doubtful.

alignments.label: After wounds

britannica.quote: it often follows wounds and operations

wikipedia.quote: enter through a break in the skin, such as a wound, a scratch or a surgical cut

alignments.note: Both link the disease to wounds. Wikipedia explains the link: bacteria enter through the break in the skin. Inference: the hospital outbreaks of 1810 fit bacteria passing between patients.

alignments.label: Bleeding and purging

britannica.quote: The cure consists in bleeding, in purging with saline medicines

wikipedia.quote: The usual treatment is an antibiotic, most often penicillin

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. Penicillin replaced bleeding and purging, which do not act on the infection.

alignments.label: When it can kill
alignments.note: Before antibiotics the disease could kill. Today serious complications such as sepsis are uncommon. The change comes from treatment.

alignments.label: Which layer of skin

wikipedia.quote: a bacterial infection of the upper layers of the skin

alignments.note: The 1810 entry calls it an inflammation of the skin. Wikipedia names the upper layers, which sets it apart from cellulitis.

suggestedQuestions: Is St Anthony's fire the same as erysipelas?
What did the 1810 entry think caused erysipelas?

Is St Anthony's fire the same as erysipe.answer: The 1810 entry uses the name for erysipelas [B1] and says it comes from the saint invoked against it [B5]. Wikipedia agrees that erysipelas was called St Anthony's fire, but notes that the same name was also used for ergotism, a different illness caused by rye infected with a fungus [W7]. So the name pointed to two diseases.

What did the 1810 entry think caused ery.answer: An acrid bile thrown upon the skin from a disordered stomach and liver [B4]. Wikipedia says most cases are caused by the bacterium Streptococcus pyogenes [W3], which usually enters through a break in the skin such as a wound [W4]. The 1810 entry did note that it often follows wounds and operations in hospitals [B6].
